134.title: Pradakshina
134.howItsDone: After darshan, many Hindus walk clockwise around the inner shrine of a temple, keeping the deity on their right, and some also circle sacred trees, the tulsi plant, or holy hills such as Arunachala; at home, some turn once in place at the end of puja.

segments.voice: Yesterday, darshan: to see and to be seen. Your line was see.

Ganesha and his brother Kartikeya are told that whoever circles the world first wins. You met this race back on day twenty-five. Kartikeya jumps on his peacock and flies off across oceans and mountains. Ganesha, on his little mouse, simply walks around his parents, Shiva and Parvati, and says: you are my world. He wins. Children love that story. It's also a set of instructions, because Hindus walk around what they love all the time. Around shrines. Around trees. Around whole mountains. Today: pradakshina.
screen: `GANESHA CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.` → `YOU ARE MY WORLD.` → `TODAY: PRADAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: Pradakshina means walking around something holy, clockwise. The direction is inside the word: dakshina means the right hand, the right side. So you walk keeping the sacred on your right, the side of respect, with the center always in the center. After darshan at the front of the temple, many people turn and walk around the inner shrine, and many temples build a path for exactly this, a corridor that loops around the sanctum. Some people do one round, some three, some more, often a number that's meaningful to them or their family. It doesn't stop at the temple walls. People circle the sacred tulsi plant in the courtyard, or a great fig tree. Some circle whole mountains. At Arunachala, in Tamil Nadu, pilgrims walk all the way around the holy hill, many miles, often barefoot, often at night under the full moon. Even a Hindu wedding has a circle at its heart: the couple walks around the sacred fire. Why a circle? A straight line goes somewhere else. A circle keeps coming back to the same center. Every step, the holy is right there beside you, and you can't lose sight of it. And there's Ganesha's point: the thing you circle becomes your world. At the end of home puja, when there's no room to walk, some people simply turn once in place, clockwise. The same act, made small. The center stays the center.
screen: `DAKSHINA: THE RIGHT SIDE.` · `A PATH AROUND THE SANCTUM.` · `TREES, FIRE, WHOLE MOUNTAINS.` · `A CIRCLE KEEPS THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, and choose a center: a chair, a table, your corner, or just the spot where you were sitting. Walk slowly around it clockwise, keeping it on your right, one round, or three if there's room; with no room, turn once in place, and if walking is hard today, trace a slow circle with your hand. Then sit back down at the center.
Pradakshina. Walking clockwise around something holy, keeping it on your right, so the center stays the center. Today's word.
Your line: around. Keep the holy on your right, at the center. Day one hundred thirty-four, done.

135.title: The priest
135.hook: what he's doing at the front
135.howItsDone: In Hindu temples, the pujari performs the daily rites for the deity (bathing, dressing, food offerings and arti), and on request performs archana on a devotee's behalf, reciting the deity's names with their name and lineage; families also invite priests home for life-cycle rites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina, walking the circle clockwise, keeping the holy on your right. Your line was around.

You're at the threshold of the inner shrine. Inside, in the lamplight, a man in a white cloth, bare-chested, a thread across his shoulder, is moving fast. He's chanting in Sanskrit, almost too quickly to follow. He pours something over the image, picks up flowers, rings a bell, turns, and suddenly he's asking you something. Your name? He repeats it into the chant. Flowers go up, the flame comes out, and a spoonful of water lands in your palm. It's over in two minutes, and you have no idea what just happened. Today: the priest.
screen: `A MAN IN WHITE, CHANTING FAST.` → `HE ASKS YOUR NAME.` → `WHAT JUST HAPPENED?`

segments.voice: The word is pujari: the one who does the puja. In many temples, the priests are the only ones who go into the inner shrine. He isn't a preacher, and he isn't necessarily your guru. His job is the form: the rites, done exactly, every day. Three days ago you heard that the murti is cared for like someone living in the house. The pujari does the caring, often starting before dawn. He bathes the image with water, sometimes milk or honey, a rite called abhisheka, then dresses it, offers food, and performs arti at set times. Many of these rites follow detailed temple manuals, handed down for generations. And when you come with an offering, he acts on your behalf. He asks your name, and often your family lineage or birth star, and places them inside the Sanskrit: who is offering, when and where, and for what. Then he recites the names of the deity, sometimes a hundred and eight of them, offering a flower or a pinch of something with each. That's archana. He brings back the flame, the holy water and the prasad for you. In many large temples, priests have traditionally come from particular Brahmin families, trained from childhood, while many village and local temples have hereditary priests from other communities. In recent years, some temples and groups have also trained priests from new backgrounds, including women. Families also call a priest home for weddings, naming ceremonies and housewarmings. You don't have to know every word. Someone holds the form.
screen: `PUJARI — THE ONE WHO DOES THE PUJA.` · `BATHE, DRESS, FEED, ARTI.` · `YOUR NAME, INSIDE THE SANSKRIT.` · `SOMEONE HOLDS THE FORM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who keeps a form going so others can rely on it, whether or not anyone notices: the person who opens the building every morning, the grandmother who never misses the evening lamp, the nurse on the night shift, the teacher who arrives early. Picture them at their careful work, and if you'd like, silently thank them. Then notice that you, too, hold a small form now: a corner, a flame, a practice.
Pujari. The temple priest: the one who does the puja, every day, exactly, and offers on your behalf. Today's word.
Your line: someone holds the form. Now you know what he's doing at the front. See you tomorrow.

136.title: Bhajan
136.howItsDone: Many Hindus gather in homes and temples, often weekly, to sing bhajans, simple devotional songs in regional languages, many written by medieval poet-saints, with harmonium, drums and small cymbals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pujari, the priest at the front. Your line was someone holds the form.

It's a Saturday evening in somebody's living room. The sofas are pushed against the wall, sheets on the carpet. An uncle sits at a harmonium, pumping the bellows with one hand. A teenager drums on a dholak. An auntie has tiny brass cymbals that go ching, ching, ching. Thirty people sit on the floor. Some have lyric sheets; most don't need them. Nobody is a professional. Half of them are off-key. And by the third song, the whole room is singing so loudly the neighbors can hear. Today: bhajan.
screen: `SOFAS AGAINST THE WALL.` → `HARMONIUM, DRUM, TINY CYMBALS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM, SINGING LOUD.`

segments.voice: Bhajan is a devotional song. The word comes from the Sanskrit root bhaj: to share in, to serve, to adore. It's the same root as bhakti, your sixteenth word: devotion is a verb. A bhajan is bhakti you can sing. Bhajans are usually simple: short lines, lots of repetition, melodies anyone can pick up by the second time through. And they're in the languages people actually speak: Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Tamil, Kannada, and many more. Many were written by the poet-saints of medieval India, singers who wanted God in the everyday language of the street. Mirabai, the princess you met on day sixteen, singing for Krishna. Surdas and Tulsidas. Tukaram in Maharashtra. Their songs are still sung in living rooms and temples. Some bhajans are very short. One that many people know, sung at Gandhi's prayer meetings, begins: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram. Lord of the line of Raghu, King Ram; purifier of the fallen, Sita and Ram. Why sing in a group, and why loud? A group bhajan does something quiet prayer doesn't. Your voice disappears into everyone else's. You stop hearing whether you're good. For a few minutes, you're not a person worrying; you're part of one big sound. The tradition doesn't ask for a pretty voice. It asks for a whole one.
screen: `BHAJ: TO SHARE IN, TO ADORE.` · `SIMPLE, REPEATED, EVERYDAY WORDS.` · `THE POET-SAINTS: MIRABAI, TUKARAM.` · `NOT PRETTY. WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Sing the line, or sing inside if you're somewhere you can't: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram, once slowly, then a little louder than feels comfortable, without worrying about the tune. If you'd rather, sing any song of devotion or gratitude you already know, from any part of your life, and let the sound fill your chest. Then stop, and sit in the ringing quiet afterward.
Bhajan. A devotional song, simple and repeated, in everyday language, usually sung together, and usually loud. Today's word.
Your line: loud. Half of them are off-key, and the whole room still sings. That's day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: The seven steps
137.hook: a wedding fire, a knotted scarf, stolen shoes, and a guest asking what's actually happening
137.howItsDone: In many Hindu weddings the couple circle a sacred fire (the pheras) and take seven steps together (saptapadi) while a priest recites the vows; families differ on the number of circles and on customs like kanyadaan, the mangalsutra and sindoor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhajan: songs sung together, out loud. Your line was loud. Today, the loudest thing a Hindu family ever throws, and the quiet steps in the middle of it. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

A wedding hall, hour three. The couple sit under a canopy with a small fire between them and the priest. The groom's scarf has been knotted to the bride's sari. Two aunts are whispering about which way the knot should go. Near the door, the bride's cousins are hiding the groom's shoes and planning what to charge for them. And the groom's best friend, who didn't grow up with any of this, leans over and asks: what's actually happening? Plenty of people in that room couldn't tell him. Today: the steps in the middle.
screen: `A FIRE, A KNOTTED SCARF.` → `THE SHOES ARE MISSING.` → `WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING?`

segments.voice: The fire is Agni, and in the old wedding rites the fire is the witness. Everything important happens in front of it. In many weddings the couple walk around it, often seven times, in some communities four; these circles are the pheras. Inside or beside them is a rite called saptapadi: seven steps, taken together. An old household manual gives a wish for each step. One for food. Two for strength. Three for wealth. Four for happiness. Five for the herds, since this is a very old text. Six for the seasons. And at the seventh: with seven steps, be my friend. Of everything a wedding could promise, the last word is friend. Around it you'll see more, and families do these differently. Garlands exchanged, sometimes with the groom's friends lifting him out of reach. Kanyadaan, the bride's parents placing her hand in the groom's, which many families now do differently or reword. A mangalsutra, a necklace of black beads and gold, tied by the groom in many weddings. Sindoor, red powder, drawn into the parting of the bride's hair in many North Indian weddings. Before any of it, many families compare horoscopes, which is called kundli matching; many couples skip it. And the stolen shoes? That's joota chupai, a game, not a rite. The ransom is negotiable.
screen: `THE FIRE IS THE WITNESS.` · `SEVEN STEPS, SEVEN WISHES.` · `AT THE SEVENTH: BE MY FRIEND.` · `GARLANDS, A NECKLACE, A RED LINE.`

segments.voice: Seven breaths, seven steps. Think of someone who has walked beside you for a long time: a partner, a parent, a brother or sister, a friend. With each slow breath, take one step beside them in your mind: food, strength, wealth, happiness, the herds if you like, the seasons. On the seventh breath, just the word: friend, and sit quietly with them for a while.
Saptapadi. Seven steps, taken together before the fire; at the seventh, the couple are called friends. Today's word.
Your line: seven steps make a friend. The last vow is the plainest one. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

138.title: Satsang, in person
138.hook: finding a room in your city (verified hosts only)
138.tomorrow: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)
138.howItsDone: Many Hindus attend satsangs, regular gatherings at temples, homes or community halls that usually include devotional singing, a reading or talk, silence and prasad, followed by tea and conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven steps around a wedding fire. Your line was seven steps make a friend.

You can light a lamp alone. You can't really get married alone. This week opened at the temple steps: mandir, shoes off. Then darshan, seeing and being seen. Pradakshina, walking around. The pujari, who holds the form. Bhajan, loud. Saptapadi, seven steps around a fire. Under all of them: other people. And there's a word you learned way back on day twenty, in the first camp, for exactly this. Back then it was an idea. Today, it's an address, a time, and a door you actually walk through. Today: satsang, in person.
screen: `YOU CAN'T GET MARRIED ALONE.` → `A WEEK OF OTHER PEOPLE.` → `TODAY: SATSANG, IN PERSON.`

segments.voice: Satsang joins two words. Sat means true, real, good, what actually is. Sang means company, being together. So satsang is the company of the true, or good company, and your line from day twenty still holds: good company changes you. A satsang can be a group in a temple hall on a Sunday, a few families in a living room reading a chapter of the Gita, a student group on a campus, a weekly bhajan evening. Many follow a similar shape: some singing, a reading or a short talk, maybe questions, a few minutes of silence, prasad, and often tea afterward, which is where people become friends. So how do you find a good room? Start with what's established and public. Ask at a local temple; many have a notice board or a front desk. Ask a Hindu friend or coworker where their family goes. Look for groups that meet in open places and have been around for years. And a few honest signs to walk away: a group that pressures you to come back, asks for large sums of money, wants to cut you off from family or friends, or says only its teacher can be trusted. Good company doesn't grab. It welcomes, and lets you leave. You won't love every room, and the first may feel awkward: you won't know the songs or when to stand. That's normal. Sit in the back, sing what you can, stay for the tea. Everything you practiced this week, the shoes, the bow, the songs, was preparation for this.
screen: `SAT + SANG: THE COMPANY OF THE TRUE.` · `SINGING, READING, SILENCE, TEA.` · `START ESTABLISHED AND PUBLIC.` · `GOOD COMPANY DOESN'T GRAB.`

segments.voice: Think of one place near you where people might gather like this, a temple, a community center, a campus, a friend's family, and if you don't know any, picture asking one person who might. Choose one to try in the next month, and picture the evening: shoes off, a spot at the back, someone smiling as they pass you a lyric sheet. You sing the parts you can, and afterward someone hands you a cup of tea.
Satsang. The company of the true: people gathering to sing, read, sit in silence and share tea, and the good company that changes you. Today's word.
Your line: go. That's the week; tomorrow, the festivals begin with Diwali, the biggest of them.

139.title: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)
139.hook: five days of light begin: a clean house, something new, and a demon defeated before dawn
139.carry: clean house, clean body, the darkness defeated
139.tomorrow: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)
139.howItsDone: In the days before Diwali, many Hindu families clean their homes thoroughly; on Dhanteras they buy something new, often a metal utensil or coin, and light a lamp for Yama in the evening; on Naraka Chaturdashi many, especially in South India and Maharashtra, rise before dawn for an oil bath and new clothes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, satsang, in person: the company of the true. Your line was go.

A week before, it starts in the corners. Mothers and grandmothers pull everything off the shelves. Curtains washed, cupboards emptied, the dusty box under the bed finally dealt with. Kids grumbling. Then the shopping: a new steel pot, a silver coin, new clothes. Then patterns of colored powder on the doorstep. And finally the lamps, rows and rows of them on every windowsill and balcony, until the whole street glows. For three weeks you've built a practice at home and in the temple. Now the calendar takes over, and the practices become festivals. The biggest comes first. Today: Diwali.
screen: `THE HOUSE, TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.` → `A NEW POT, A SILVER COIN.` → `THEN, LAMPS ON EVERY SILL.`

segments.voice: You know the name by now: a row of lamps, your deepa from day one hundred and twelve, multiplied by a whole country. What's new is the calendar. Diwali falls in autumn, around the new moon, the darkest night of the month, usually in October or November. And for many families it's five days, not one; today, the first two. Different regions tell different stories. You met the one many North Indians tell on day sixty-nine: Rama coming home to Ayodhya, and the city lighting lamps to guide him. Jains and Sikhs mark their own observances in the same season. Day one is Dhanteras. Dhan means wealth, teras the thirteenth lunar day. The house has been cleaned, and now people buy something new, often metal: a pot, a spoon, a coin. It's also the day of Dhanvantari, physician of the gods, who in the old story rose from the churning ocean carrying the pot of nectar. In the evening, many families set one lamp outside, facing south, for Yama, the lord of death, asking him to pass the house by. Day two is Naraka Chaturdashi, the fourteenth. A demon king, Narakasura, had grown so cruel he'd imprisoned thousands. Krishna, and in many tellings his queen Satyabhama beside him, defeated him and set the prisoners free. In much of South India and Maharashtra, this is the big morning. People rise before dawn, rub their bodies with oil, bathe, put on new clothes, and the first firecrackers go off in the dark. Clean house, clean body, the darkness defeated. The stage is set for the new moon.
screen: `FIVE DAYS, NOT ONE.` · `DHANTERAS: SOMETHING NEW.` · `A LAMP FOR YAMA, FACING SOUTH.` · `NARAKA CHATURDASHI: DARKNESS DEFEATED.`

segments.voice: Find one small cluttered thing within reach, a drawer, a desk corner, your phone's home screen, and take one minute to clear it. Then sit, and picture a single lamp on your front step, glowing outward into the dark street. If you pray, think of the name you honor coming home; if not, just picture the light, waiting for whoever arrives.
Diwali. The festival of lamps, five days long: it begins with a clean house, something new, and a demon defeated before dawn. Today's word.
Your line: clean house, clean body, the darkness defeated. The darkest night comes next. Day one hundred thirty-nine, done.

140.title: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)
140.hook: a hill of food stacked before dawn: Lakshmi at the door, a mountain lifted, a sister's blessing
140.carry: a mountain held like an umbrella
140.howItsDone: On the new-moon night of Diwali many Hindu families perform Lakshmi puja with Ganesha, light lamps throughout the home and draw Lakshmi's footprints at the door; the next day temples offer annakut for Govardhan puja, and on Bhai Dooj sisters mark their brothers' foreheads with tilak and share a meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali began: a clean house, something new on Dhanteras, a lamp for Yama, and Narakasura defeated before dawn. Your line was clean house, clean body, the darkness defeated.

Before dawn, a temple kitchen is already roaring, while the lamps from the big night still smoke on the windowsills. Rice, lentils, vegetables, sweets, dish after dish, carried out in steel pans and stacked on the steps in front of the image until the food is shaped like a small hill. Children wait for their share and hear the story while they wait: a boy who once lifted a real hill. Across town, a sister is already planning tomorrow's plate for her brother. The lamps were only the middle of Diwali. Today, the last three days.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, A TEMPLE KITCHEN.` → `FOOD STACKED LIKE A HILL.` → `THE LAMPS WERE ONLY THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Day three is Lakshmi puja, on the new moon itself, the night you met on day eighty-eight: the clean house, the open door, the little footprints walking in. Ganesha is honored beside Lakshmi, and first, as always: clear the road, then begin. In Bengal it belongs to Kali, the fierce mother. In Gujarat, the new year begins the next morning. Day four is Govardhan puja. In the Bhagavata Purana, young Krishna persuaded the cowherds of Vraj to honor their own hill, Govardhan, which fed their cows, instead of the storm god Indra. Indra, offended, sent rain for days. And Krishna lifted the whole hill with one hand, a single finger in many tellings, and held it up like an umbrella while everyone sheltered underneath. So temples build a mountain of food, called annakut, and share it. Day five is Bhai Dooj, for brothers and sisters. A sister marks her brother's forehead with a tilak, prays for his long life, and feeds him; he gives her a gift. The story behind it: Yama, lord of death, visited his sister Yamuna on this day and was welcomed with a meal. Notice the bookends. Diwali opened with a lamp for Yama, asking death to pass by. It closes with Yama as a brother, sitting down to eat. Five days: a clean house, darkness beaten, fortune welcomed, shelter under a lifted mountain, and family at the table.
screen: `LAKSHMI PUJA: GANESHA FIRST.` · `GOVARDHAN: THE HILL HELD UP.` · `BHAI DOOJ: A SISTER'S BLESSING.` · `YAMA AT THE START AND AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Think back to a stretch when things were pouring down on you, and someone held something up so you could get through: a parent who took the extra shift, a friend who covered for you, a teacher who stayed late. Picture them standing there, holding it, and breathe out slowly under the shelter. Then let one more face come, someone who's like a brother or sister to you, and wish them a long life, the way a sister does on Bhai Dooj.
Diwali. Five days of light: something new, darkness defeated, Lakshmi welcomed on the darkest night, a mountain lifted, and siblings at the table. Today's word.
Your line: a mountain held like an umbrella. Diwali's five days are done. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit lakṣmī: fortune, prosperity, well-being; the goddess welcomed on Diwali night.

what it means: five days that move from a clean house to darkness defeated, fortune welcomed, shelter given and family fed.

what a scholar hears: Govardhan's lifting is told in Bhagavata Purana 10.24–25; the Yama–Yamuna story behind Bhai Dooj (Yama Dvitiya) is found in later Puranic and regional tradition; Bengal keeps Kali puja on the same new moon.
